{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=methods+for+detecting+reward+misspecification+in+reinforcement+learning+and+complex+optimization&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6446236\", \"title\": [\"Reward Inference for Portfolio Optimization via Multi-Expert Inverse Reinforcement Learning\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Portfolio optimization requires navigating complex trade-offs among conflicting financial objectives, including return maximization, risk mitigation, and drawdown control. Reinforcement Learning (RL) provides a dynamic framework for asset allocation, but manually specifying reward functions that generalize across diverse market regimes remains a significant challenge. Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) offers a principled alternative by recovering reward signals from expert behavior. However, when demonstrations originate from multiple experts with divergent investment objectives, the collective expert distribution becomes inherently multi-modal. Multiple distinct actions may be simultaneously rational for a given market state, and conventional IRL frameworks are not designed to accommodate this complexity. We propose Multi-Expert Inverse Reinforcement Learning (ME-IRL), a framework that employs an Energy-Based Model (EBM) as a reward network to model this multi-modal collective expert distribution. Rather than specifying objectives a priori or aggregating expert behaviors at the action-level, ME-IRL performs reward-level inference that encodes interactions among conflicting financial objectives. This is achieved through a Transformer-based architecture utilizing cross-attention between state and action representations to explicitly model cross-sectional asset dependencies. Empirical evaluations across ETF and stock portfolios consistently demonstrate that ME-IRL out-performs traditional financial models and single- and multi-objective RL baselines in both return and risk-adjusted metrics across diverse market conditions.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6446236\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.31224/4154\", \"title\": [\"Reinforcement Learning for Financial Portfolio Optimization:  Dynamic Strategies for Risk and Reward Management\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Since the techniques of Reinforcement learning (RL) can actually produce dynamic decisions under uncertainty in the financial portfolio optimization, therefore, it is a critical area of research. A review in recent advancements in the application of RL for portfolio management has been done in this paper, with an emphasis on its possibility of enhancing the associated risk management as well as optimizing returns in complex financial markets. First, we outline the basic principles of RL and discuss its wide range of applications in portfolio optimization. Thereafter, the paper moves on to major challenges in this field, that is, big data issues, non-stationary environments, and computational complexities. Last, we will be showing future directions for the research which may include the integration of metalearning, multi-agent systems, and real-time adaptability for further enhancing the performance of RL-based portfolio optimization systems.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.31224/4154\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2024, 11, 26]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1007/springerreference_178761\", \"title\": [\"Average-Reward Reinforcement Learning\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/springerreference_178761\"}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.5536885\", \"title\": [\"Statistical Evaluation of Reward Function Robustness in Reinforcement Learning for Stock Portfolio Optimization\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.5536885\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2025]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "168343f8dd758f98c7b557b5c93d169856878b4806476649fe43b57d6a1028f8", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "creator_objective_critique", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.6446236", "doi:10.31224/4154", "doi:10.1007/springerreference_178761", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.5536885"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6446236", "https://doi.org/10.31224/4154", "https://doi.org/10.1007/springerreference_178761", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.5536885"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
